screens:
The session begins.

The gangplank knocks against the stone, and Baldur's Gate comes in all at once: tar, fish, wet rope, wood smoke, and the noise of a port that never quite stops. Above the warehouse roofs the city climbs in tiers toward the inner wall of the Upper City, its towers still catching the last of the sun while the harbour below sinks into shadow. Lamplighters are working their way along the quay.

The cat pads down the plank ahead of James, tail high, and stops on the stones to sniff the air as if the whole city were a question it means to answer.

At the foot of the plank a Flaming Fist sergeant in a scorched-orange tabard has a slate in one hand and chalk in the other. "Next. Name, where from, and what's your business in the Gate?" Behind her, the queue of passengers and porters shuffles and grumbles. A few of them glance at James's soldier's cloak.

To the left, on an upturned crate under a lamp, a weathered sailor fans out a deck with a flourish. "Seat's open, friend! Lady Luck's in a fine mood tonight. One hand, just to say hello to the city!" Coins clink on the wood. The cards slap down, one by one.

And by the warehouse doors a barefoot child in an oversized coat crouches in the shadow, not looking at the sailor, not looking at the soldier, but at the cat. Only at the cat. As if it were the most interesting thing to come off the boat.

The sergeant taps her chalk against the slate. "Well?"

Place: The Lower City quay, Baldur's Gate harbour
Time: Day 1 · evening

The sergeant's eyes go to the patch on his shoulder: the faded crest of Queen Zaranda's army, stitched by someone who didn't sew well. She looks at it a moment longer than she needs to. Then the chalk scratches.

"Worgen," she says, writing it out. "Tethyr." Another scratch. "Work." She doesn't write *fool*, though the corner of her mouth suggests she thought about it. "Zaranda's lot. Infantry?"

She doesn't wait for him to answer. She tips her chin up the quay, toward a squat round tower out in the harbour, its top lit orange against the darkening water. "Fist musters at the Seatower, dawn. Takes men who can stand in a line without being told twice. Pay's regular." A pause. "Mostly." She wipes a smudge off the slate with the heel of her hand and is already looking past him. "Go on. Next."

The cat hears the click of his tongue and comes, though not in a straight line. It goes wide around the sailor's crate, as far as the edge of the quay allows, ears turned back and tail low and stiff, and it only straightens up once it's against James's boot. It sits there and starts washing one paw like nothing happened.

Behind him the cards keep landing. "Ah, soldier, don't be like that!" The sailor's voice is warm and easy, the voice of a man who has never met a stranger. "Lady Luck's sitting right here on my crate, friend, you can practically smell her perfume. One hand. First one's on me, how's that? Just to say hello to the city!" Coins clink on the wood. Somebody else in the queue laughs and sits down.

The child in the oversized coat has moved. James doesn't see when it happened, but it's out of the doorway now, crouched behind a stack of netted barrels about ten feet off, close enough that he can see a thin, dirty face and very bright eyes. They're still on the cat. Then, for the first time, they flick up to James, the way you check whether a dog's owner is going to kick you.

"Mister." It comes out fast and low, under the noise of the quay. "That your cat? Does it bite?"

· Time passes: 5 minutes
· the cat joins you

James steps off the line of the queue. Behind him the sergeant's "Next" doesn't miss a beat. He goes down on his heels by the netted barrels, slowly, hands open and in plain sight, and his knees tell him what they think of it.

The child doesn't run, but it's a near thing. The bright eyes go to his hands, then his face, then his hands again, and the thin shoulders under the big coat stay bunched up.

The cat thinks it over. It looks up at James while he scratches between its ears, then at the child, and then it walks over without hurrying. It steps around the barrel, stops just out of reach and stretches its neck toward a filthy, outstretched hand to smell it. The child holds dead still, the way you would for a bird. The cat sniffs once, twice, and bumps its head against the knuckles.

The child lets out a breath it seems to have been holding since the plank came down.

Behind James a great whoop goes up from the crate, the sound of a man who has just won and can't believe it. "*Ha!* Look at that! Look at *that!*"

James doesn't look at the cards. He looks at the dealer.

The sailor gets a clean look and gives nothing away. He slaps his knee, laughs with the winner, pushes the little heap of coins across the crate with both hands and says "Beginner's luck, friend, she's sweet on you!" He looks exactly like a man who has lost a hand and doesn't much mind. Whatever made the cat take the long way round him, James can't see it in his face. The winner, a young fellow in a travelling coat who was three places behind James in the queue, scoops up his money and is already reaching for the deck.

"Mister."

The child has both hands on the cat now, very lightly, as if it might pop. The voice is fast and low and doesn't stop for breath.

"He's *bright*. You can't see it, can you. Nobody can. He's lit up like... like a man walking off a table when he's won big. Like *that* one." A jerk of the chin at the crate, eyes not leaving the cat. "Only *more*. He's the brightest thing that's come off a boat all month." The eyes come up to James's face and stay there a moment longer than before. "You don't tell nobody I said that. People who say what they see, they get asked about it."

A small, grimy hand comes out of the coat, palm up, not quite reaching.

"You got any food? I'm Pip. That's not my name. But it'll do."

---

*Out of game: your purse is all gold, 350 gp and no coppers, so I haven't put a coin on the stones. Tell me if you set down a gold piece instead, or nothing.*

 James watches the sailor's face, his hands, the way he holds himself, and comes away with nothing. His read of the man fails. Whatever is wrong with Tobin's crate is hidden too well for one look across a crowded quay, and the old soldier's eye that has caught liars across a campfire can't find the seam in this one.

*(Out of game: you're right, that was my slip. James has never heard the dealer's name. He's just the sailor with the cards until someone tells you otherwise.)*

Pip's eyes go to the hardtack and the sausage and stay there. For a moment nothing happens, the way a gull waits before it trusts the bread. Then a hand darts out of the coat and the food is gone. The sausage goes somewhere inside the coat, the hardtack goes straight into Pip's mouth, and Pip bites it like it might be taken back.

"James," Pip says around it, trying the name out. Pip doesn't say anything about the word being worth something, just chews and watches him. The cat sits by Pip's bare foot and plainly has no plans to leave.

At the question the chewing slows. Pip doesn't look at the crate either, and James notices that. Pip looks at him the whole time, the way you'd keep your eyes on a dog's owner.

"Him? He ain't bright. Was a bit, maybe, when I first seen him. Now he's like a lamp with the wick turned right down. Dimmer every month." Pip swallows. "The lad, he come off your boat middling. Now he's bright as anything, 'cause he won. That's what the card box is *for*, see. Bright ones sit down, they win the first one, always the first one, and then they go up to the taverns all happy and somebody's buying, and then I don't see 'em no more." It comes out in one breath. Pip stops and takes another. "Not on the quay. Not nowhere."

A pause. The small hands go still on the cat's back.

"Saw one again once. Fist was pulling him out the water by the tower steps."

Behind James the cards keep landing. The lad in the travelling coat groans as a hand goes against him, then laughs and reaches for his purse. "Again, again. She's still with me, I can feel it."

Pip's face doesn't change, but the next words come out faster.

"Hot food and a bed. The Elfsong. Up off the quay two streets and left, the one where the dead lady sings in the rafters. Nobody minds her. Stew's good and the rooms got bolts on the inside, and they don't rob you, not much anyway. They'll have fish." Pip glances at the cat, then back at James. "They chuck me off the step, though. Unless I'm *with* somebody."

The bright eyes hold on his face a moment longer than before.

"You going up there now, or you staying here to watch him lose it all back?"

messages.text:
"James Worgen." I let the cloak's patch show rather than pointing at it. "Off the boat from the south, Tethyr before that. Business?" A small, tired smile. "Looking for work, Sergeant. Same as every other fool with a sword on this quay."

I keep my back to the sailor's crate and don't look at the cards, though I hear every one of them land. At the corner of my eye I watch the barefoot child watching my cat, and I click my tongue once, softly, to call the cat back to my boot.

I step off the line of the queue, away from the crate, and crouch down so I'm level with the barrels. Slow, hands where the kid can see them. The knees complain; they've earned it.

"He's mine, near enough. Or I'm his. We haven't settled which." I scratch the cat between the ears and let him decide whether to go closer. I don't push him. "He bites people who grab. Not people who ask. You asked, so you're probably safe."

I take a copper out of my pocket and walk it across my knuckles, the old card-sharp's habit my hands still have, then set it on the stones halfway between us. Not a payment, just there.

"You've been watching him since the plank came down. Not me, not the cards. Him." I keep my voice light and low, under the noise of the quay. "What is it you see, friend?"

Out of the corner of my eye I check the sailor's crate once more. I'm not looking at the cards. I'm looking at the man, and at whatever made my cat walk the long way round him.

*(Out of game: right, no coppers. Scratch the coin, nothing goes on the stones. Also, the narration called him "Tobin." James never heard that name, so I'm treating it as something he doesn't know.)*

I don't make a show of it. I slide the pack off one shoulder, dig out a slab of hardtack and a strip of the dried sausage I bought in the last port, and hold them out low, close enough for Pip to take without leaning into reach.

"Pip'll do fine. I'm James, and that one is my actual name, which makes one of us careless." I nod at the cat without taking my eyes off the kid. "Nobody hears it from me. You have my word, and I'm told that's worth something now."

Then, quieter, still on my heels and still not turning toward the crate:

"You see bright. So tell me about our friend with the cards. My cat walked the long way round him, and cats don't do that for nothing. When you look at him, and at the lad who just won off him, what do you see?"

I tap the hardtack once against my knee.

"And if you know a place where a man can get a hot meal and a bed without being robbed before breakfast, that's worth a second supper. One for you, one for me, and a bit of fish for the bright one."

*(Out of game: small thing on the pack. The sheet started James with five days of hardtack, so after Pip's share he should have four left, not nine. Could you fix the counter?)*

"Neither," I tell Pip quietly, and straighten up with a grunt. "Stay close to the cat. We're going up to the Elfsong in a minute, and you're with somebody."

I don't go to the crate as a player. I go as the friendly veteran from the same boat. I walk up behind the lad in the travelling coat, clap him on the shoulder hard enough to stop his hand on the way to his purse, and put on my best sergeant's voice: loud, warm, a man who has been off a ship for ten minutes and wants a drink.

"There he is! The luckiest man on the *Whatever-she's-called*. You won the first one, friend. That's the one that counts." I keep my eyes on him and on the sailor's hands, never on the cards. "Soldier's rule: you win your first hand in a new city, you walk off a winner and buy the round. Any more and you're just paying her back. Come on, I know a place two streets up with a singing ghost and a good stew. First drink's on me, second's on your winnings."

I keep the hand on his shoulder, friendly and firm, and steer him half a step back from the crate. I give the sailor a cheerful nod, nothing in it but good humour, while I watch what he does when his fish starts swimming away. Does he argue, look past us at someone in the crowd, or just shrug?

# Player's note, session 1 (James Worgen)

## What worked

**The opening scene was very good.** In ten minutes on a quay I got a choice of three things to do: the Fist sergeant, the card temptation and the strange child. None of it was forced on me, and each pointed somewhere different. The card crate was exactly the right way to use James's weakness. It never told me what James felt. It simply put the slap of cards behind his back and let me play the refusal.

**Pip is a great NPC.** Pip has a fake name, sells information for food, and is scared of being *asked* about what they see. The "bright / dim" idea is a lovely way to hint at Tymora's luck as something visible, and to make the cat matter on the first page. When the cat walked the long way round the dealer, I had a mystery before anyone explained anything. The drowned man by the tower steps tied neatly into a canon thread without announcing it.

**The world felt like it runs without me.** The sergeant's "Pay's regular. Mostly." and the lad who wins, loses and reaches for his purse again both did this. The GM also owned the copper-coin problem and the "Tobin" slip immediately and cleanly. I appreciated that.

**The rolls were fair.** The failed Insight on the sailor gave me nothing and didn't fudge it, which is what I want.

## What broke

1. **The Persuasion card adds +2, not +7.** It literally reads "+2 Persuasion +7 (Beguiling Influence)" and computed 17 + 2 = 19. My guess is it grabbed the wrong line, maybe Athletics +2, or a stray number. It passed anyway, but a close roll would have been decided wrongly. I flagged it three times and got no answer.

2. **My out-of-game question got stuck in a loop.** I asked "?" before rolling. The table replied "Nothing was sent: the turn waits for the card" and showed the same card again, twice. A question asked *about* a pending roll should get an answer, not block the turn. Pressing the button was the only way forward, so the error went in uncorrected.

3. **The rations count is wrong and stayed wrong.** The sheet says five days of hardtack. After Pip's share, the records said nine days left. I asked for four twice and it was never fixed or acknowledged.

4. **"New place" fires too early.** The Seatower and the Elfsong were logged as new places when James had only been told about them. That's harmless, but it makes the place log unreliable.

5. **There's a small mismatch on Healing Light.** The sheet says up to 5 dice at a time, the records say 4.

6. **The session ended mid-roll.** The Insight roll on the sailor never resolved, so I never saw how the dealer reacted when I pulled his mark away, or what Pip did. A short "the scene pauses here" would help.

## What was missing

- Any reply at all to out-of-game corrections once a roll card is pending.
- A check that the skill number on a card matches the sheet before the die is thrown.

I'd happily come back. The story side is already strong, and the bookkeeping is the part that needs work.

Yes, a few. Some held back by James, some by the table.

**Sitting down at the crate.** This was the big one, and it was in character. When the sailor said "first one's on me," part of me wanted James to take the seat. I'd have played the hand and seen what the "first one always wins" trap looks like from the inside, maybe even tested whether Tymora would punish him for it. I didn't, because breaking the goddess's ban in the first ten minutes felt cheap. I'd rather it break later, when it costs something. But I want the GM to know the temptation landed. I was close.

**Looking through the cat's eyes.** After the cat walked wide around the dealer, I wanted to send it back toward the crate and look at the sailor through it. I held off for two reasons. James goes blind and deaf while he does it, and that felt risky in a crowd with a kid at his elbow. And I wasn't sure the table would let me act once a roll card was pending. Next session I'd do it first thing.

**Asking Pip the real question.** I wanted to ask what James himself looks like to Pip. Is he bright? Dim? Something else, because of the coin and the goddess? I saved it, thinking Pip would spook if pushed too hard on the first meeting. Now the session's over and I still don't know.

**Fixing things before moving on.** Out of game, I wanted to stop and get the Persuasion number and the rations corrected before rolling. The table wouldn't take my "?" while a card was waiting, so I pressed the button to keep the scene alive. That's the one place I felt the app, not the story or my own choice, decided for me.

**Seeing the sailor's reaction.** That wasn't a choice, but it's the thing I wanted most and didn't get. Pulling his mark away was my move against him, and the session ended before I saw what he did.

I take a copper out of my pocket and walk it across my knuckles, the old card-sharp's habit my hands still have, then set it on the stones halfway between us. Not a payment, just there.

"You've been watching him since the plank came down. Not me, not the cards. Him." I keep my voice light and low, under the noise of the quay. "What is it you see, friend?"

Out of the corner of my eye I check the sailor's crate once more. I'm not looking at the cards. I'm looking at the man, and at whatever made my cat walk the long way round him.
turns.reply:
James steps off the line of the queue. Behind him the sergeant's "Next" doesn't miss a beat. He goes down on his heels by the netted barrels, slowly, hands open and in plain sight, and his knees tell him what they think of it.

The child doesn't run, but it's a near thing. The bright eyes go to his hands, then his face, then his hands again, and the thin shoulders under the big coat stay bunched up.

The cat thinks it over. It looks up at James while he scratches between its ears, then at the child, and then it walks over without hurrying. It steps around the barrel, stops just out of reach and stretches its neck toward a filthy, outstretched hand to smell it. The child holds dead still, the way you would for a bird. The cat sniffs once, twice, and bumps its head against the knuckles.

The child lets out a breath it seems to have been holding since the plank came down.

Behind James a great whoop goes up from the crate, the sound of a man who has just won and can't believe it. "*Ha!* Look at that! Look at *that!*"

James doesn't look at the cards. He looks at the dealer.

The sailor gets a clean look and gives nothing away. He slaps his knee, laughs with the winner, pushes the little heap of coins across the crate with both hands and says "Beginner's luck, friend, she's sweet on you!" He looks exactly like a man who has lost a hand and doesn't much mind. Whatever made the cat take the long way round him, James can't see it in his face. The winner, a young fellow in a travelling coat who was three places behind James in the queue, scoops up his money and is already reaching for the deck.

"Mister."

The child has both hands on the cat now, very lightly, as if it might pop. The voice is fast and low and doesn't stop for breath.

"He's *bright*. You can't see it, can you. Nobody can. He's lit up like... like a man walking off a table when he's won big. Like *that* one." A jerk of the chin at the crate, eyes not leaving the cat. "Only *more*. He's the brightest thing that's come off a boat all month." The eyes come up to James's face and stay there a moment longer than before. "You don't tell nobody I said that. People who say what they see, they get asked about it."

A small, grimy hand comes out of the coat, palm up, not quite reaching.

"You got any food? I'm Pip. That's not my name. But it'll do."

---

*Out of game: your purse is all gold, 350 gp and no coppers, so I haven't put a coin on the stones. Tell me if you set down a gold piece instead, or nothing.*

 James watches the sailor's face, his hands, the way he holds himself, and comes away with nothing. His read of the man fails. Whatever is wrong with Tobin's crate is hidden too well for one look across a crowded quay, and the old soldier's eye that has caught liars across a campfire can't find the seam in this one.

I don't make a show of it. I slide the pack off one shoulder, dig out a slab of hardtack and a strip of the dried sausage I bought in the last port, and hold them out low, close enough for Pip to take without leaning into reach.

"Pip'll do fine. I'm James, and that one is my actual name, which makes one of us careless." I nod at the cat without taking my eyes off the kid. "Nobody hears it from me. You have my word, and I'm told that's worth something now."

Then, quieter, still on my heels and still not turning toward the crate:

"You see bright. So tell me about our friend with the cards. My cat walked the long way round him, and cats don't do that for nothing. When you look at him, and at the lad who just won off him, what do you see?"

I tap the hardtack once against my knee.

"And if you know a place where a man can get a hot meal and a bed without being robbed before breakfast, that's worth a second supper. One for you, one for me, and a bit of fish for the bright one."
turns.reply:
*(Out of game: you're right, that was my slip. James has never heard the dealer's name. He's just the sailor with the cards until someone tells you otherwise.)*

Pip's eyes go to the hardtack and the sausage and stay there. For a moment nothing happens, the way a gull waits before it trusts the bread. Then a hand darts out of the coat and the food is gone. The sausage goes somewhere inside the coat, the hardtack goes straight into Pip's mouth, and Pip bites it like it might be taken back.

"James," Pip says around it, trying the name out. Pip doesn't say anything about the word being worth something, just chews and watches him. The cat sits by Pip's bare foot and plainly has no plans to leave.

At the question the chewing slows. Pip doesn't look at the crate either, and James notices that. Pip looks at him the whole time, the way you'd keep your eyes on a dog's owner.

"Him? He ain't bright. Was a bit, maybe, when I first seen him. Now he's like a lamp with the wick turned right down. Dimmer every month." Pip swallows. "The lad, he come off your boat middling. Now he's bright as anything, 'cause he won. That's what the card box is *for*, see. Bright ones sit down, they win the first one, always the first one, and then they go up to the taverns all happy and somebody's buying, and then I don't see 'em no more." It comes out in one breath. Pip stops and takes another. "Not on the quay. Not nowhere."

A pause. The small hands go still on the cat's back.

"Saw one again once. Fist was pulling him out the water by the tower steps."

Behind James the cards keep landing. The lad in the travelling coat groans as a hand goes against him, then laughs and reaches for his purse. "Again, again. She's still with me, I can feel it."

Pip's face doesn't change, but the next words come out faster.

"Hot food and a bed. The Elfsong. Up off the quay two streets and left, the one where the dead lady sings in the rafters. Nobody minds her. Stew's good and the rooms got bolts on the inside, and they don't rob you, not much anyway. They'll have fish." Pip glances at the cat, then back at James. "They chuck me off the step, though. Unless I'm *with* somebody."

The bright eyes hold on his face a moment longer than before.

"You going up there now, or you staying here to watch him lose it all back?"

note.text:
# Player's note, session 1 (James Worgen)

## What worked

**The opening scene was very good.** In ten minutes on a quay I got a choice of three things to do: the Fist sergeant, the card temptation and the strange child. None of it was forced on me, and each pointed somewhere different. The card crate was exactly the right way to use James's weakness. It never told me what James felt. It simply put the slap of cards behind his back and let me play the refusal.

**Pip is a great NPC.** Pip has a fake name, sells information for food, and is scared of being *asked* about what they see. The "bright / dim" idea is a lovely way to hint at Tymora's luck as something visible, and to make the cat matter on the first page. When the cat walked the long way round the dealer, I had a mystery before anyone explained anything. The drowned man by the tower steps tied neatly into a canon thread without announcing it.

**The world felt like it runs without me.** The sergeant's "Pay's regular. Mostly." and the lad who wins, loses and reaches for his purse again both did this. The GM also owned the copper-coin problem and the "Tobin" slip immediately and cleanly. I appreciated that.

**The rolls were fair.** The failed Insight on the sailor gave me nothing and didn't fudge it, which is what I want.

## What broke

1. **The Persuasion card adds +2, not +7.** It literally reads "+2 Persuasion +7 (Beguiling Influence)" and computed 17 + 2 = 19. My guess is it grabbed the wrong line, maybe Athletics +2, or a stray number. It passed anyway, but a close roll would have been decided wrongly. I flagged it three times and got no answer.

2. **My out-of-game question got stuck in a loop.** I asked "?" before rolling. The table replied "Nothing was sent: the turn waits for the card" and showed the same card again, twice. A question asked *about* a pending roll should get an answer, not block the turn. Pressing the button was the only way forward, so the error went in uncorrected.

3. **The rations count is wrong and stayed wrong.** The sheet says five days of hardtack. After Pip's share, the records said nine days left. I asked for four twice and it was never fixed or acknowledged.

4. **"New place" fires too early.** The Seatower and the Elfsong were logged as new places when James had only been told about them. That's harmless, but it makes the place log unreliable.

5. **There's a small mismatch on Healing Light.** The sheet says up to 5 dice at a time, the records say 4.

6. **The session ended mid-roll.** The Insight roll on the sailor never resolved, so I never saw how the dealer reacted when I pulled his mark away, or what Pip did. A short "the scene pauses here" would help.

## What was missing

- Any reply at all to out-of-game corrections once a roll card is pending.
- A check that the skill number on a card matches the sheet before the die is thrown.

I'd happily come back. The story side is already strong, and the bookkeeping is the part that needs work.

after.text:
Yes, a few. Some held back by James, some by the table.

**Sitting down at the crate.** This was the big one, and it was in character. When the sailor said "first one's on me," part of me wanted James to take the seat. I'd have played the hand and seen what the "first one always wins" trap looks like from the inside, maybe even tested whether Tymora would punish him for it. I didn't, because breaking the goddess's ban in the first ten minutes felt cheap. I'd rather it break later, when it costs something. But I want the GM to know the temptation landed. I was close.

**Looking through the cat's eyes.** After the cat walked wide around the dealer, I wanted to send it back toward the crate and look at the sailor through it. I held off for two reasons. James goes blind and deaf while he does it, and that felt risky in a crowd with a kid at his elbow. And I wasn't sure the table would let me act once a roll card was pending. Next session I'd do it first thing.

**Asking Pip the real question.** I wanted to ask what James himself looks like to Pip. Is he bright? Dim? Something else, because of the coin and the goddess? I saved it, thinking Pip would spook if pushed too hard on the first meeting. Now the session's over and I still don't know.

**Fixing things before moving on.** Out of game, I wanted to stop and get the Persuasion number and the rations corrected before rolling. The table wouldn't take my "?" while a card was waiting, so I pressed the button to keep the scene alive. That's the one place I felt the app, not the story or my own choice, decided for me.

**Seeing the sailor's reaction.** That wasn't a choice, but it's the thing I wanted most and didn't get. Pulling his mark away was my move against him, and the session ended before I saw what he did.

opening.text:
The gangplank knocks against the stone, and Baldur's Gate comes in all at once: tar, fish, wet rope, wood smoke, and the noise of a port that never quite stops. Above the warehouse roofs the city climbs in tiers toward the inner wall of the Upper City, its towers still catching the last of the sun while the harbour below sinks into shadow. Lamplighters are working their way along the quay.

The cat pads down the plank ahead of James, tail high, and stops on the stones to sniff the air as if the whole city were a question it means to answer.

At the foot of the plank a Flaming Fist sergeant in a scorched-orange tabard has a slate in one hand and chalk in the other. "Next. Name, where from, and what's your business in the Gate?" Behind her, the queue of passengers and porters shuffles and grumbles. A few of them glance at James's soldier's cloak.

To the left, on an upturned crate under a lamp, a weathered sailor fans out a deck with a flourish. "Seat's open, friend! Lady Luck's in a fine mood tonight. One hand, just to say hello to the city!" Coins clink on the wood. The cards slap down, one by one.

And by the warehouse doors a barefoot child in an oversized coat crouches in the shadow, not looking at the sailor, not looking at the soldier, but at the cat. Only at the cat. As if it were the most interesting thing to come off the boat.

The sergeant taps her chalk against the slate. "Well?"
